text: Fill in the missing agent or term for each class of mitochondrial disruption.
questions: The insecticide *rotenone:A plant-derived insecticide also used in Parkinson's disease research.* inhibits Complex I by blocking electron transfer from iron-sulphur clusters to coenzyme Q.

In *cyanide:Seen in electroplating workers, fire-smoke inhalation and cassava ingestion.* poisoning, the toxin binds to haem a3 of Complex IV, so venous blood stays bright red because oxygen cannot accept electrons.

Lipid-soluble weak acids called *uncouplers:2,4-dinitrophenol is the classic pharmacological example.* carry protons back into the matrix, raising oxygen consumption while reducing oxidative ATP synthesis.
*Oligomycin:This antibiotic blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase.* blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase, so protons cannot return through it and electron flow and oxygen use slow.

*Atractyloside/bongkrekic acid:These agents block the carrier that exchanges matrix ATP for cytosolic ADP.* blocks the ADP–ATP translocase, so ADP cannot reach ATP synthase and the same slowing occurs.

overallFeedback.feedback: Respiratory-chain inhibitors reduce electron flow through the blocked route and reduce oxidative ATP synthesis; a Complex I block permits electron entry through Complex II and other Q-linked pathways. ATP synthase blockers (oligomycin) and ADP-ATP translocase blockers (atractyloside, bongkrekic acid) both slow electron flow and oxygen use by letting the proton gradient build up unopposed. Uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient, increasing oxygen consumption under suitable conditions while reducing oxidative ATP synthesis and releasing heat; substrate-level phosphorylation can continue. Recognising the agent from the clinical pattern is essential for emergency management.
